Any number of named exports can coexist in one module; there's no limit like there is for default exports.

examples.title: A Default Export, Imported Under Any Name
examples.explanation: formatCurrency.js has exactly one default export, an anonymous function -- default exports don't need a name at the export site at all. Both fileA.js and fileB.js import that same default export, but each chooses its own local name (formatCurrency in one, money in the other) -- there's nothing wrong with either choice, and no way to detect from the name alone that they refer to the identical exported function. This is exactly the flexibility (and the refactor-safety downside) that named exports don't have.

misconceptions.description: A module can have multiple default exports, the same way it can have multiple named exports.
misconceptions.clarification: A module can have at most one default export -- attempting a second export default in the same file is a SyntaxError. Named exports have no such limit; you can export as many named values as you like from one module. If a module genuinely needs to expose several equally-important things, named exports are the correct tool, not multiple defaults (which isn't possible) and not cramming everything into one default object export (which is possible but loses most of the refactor-safety benefit named exports provide).

misconceptions.description: A variable or function declared at the top level of a module file is global, just like it would be in a plain <script> tag.
misconceptions.clarification: Each module has its own private top-level scope. A top-level const, function, or class in one file is invisible to every other file unless it's explicitly exported with the export keyword, and even then, another file must explicitly import it to gain access. This is a deliberate, meaningful difference from the old plain-<script>-tag model, where every loaded script shared one single global scope and same-named top-level declarations across different scripts could silently collide.

exercises.prompt: Given these two files, what happens when app.js runs?
hints: Look carefully at which function is exported as the default export, and which is exported as a named export -- the import statement in app.js has them backwards from what their export style requires.
Named exports must be imported inside curly braces using their exact fixed name; a default export is imported with no curly braces, under any name you choose.
shout was exported as a named export, but app.js is trying to import it as if it were the default -- what does JavaScript actually bind shout to in that case?
exercises.expectedAnswer: This throws an error (or, depending on the exact bundler/runtime, shout("hello") fails because shout is actually bound to the default export whisper, and whisper("HELLO") fails because there is no named export called whisper -- only a named export called shout exists). Either way, the import statement has the two exports' styles swapped, so nothing works as intended.
exercises.solutionExplanation: stringUtils.js exports shout as a named export and whisper as the default export -- the opposite of how app.js imports them. import shout, { whisper } from ... binds the local name shout to the module's default export (which is actually the whisper function) and tries to import a named export literally called whisper, which doesn't exist (the actual named export is called shout). Calling shout("hello") therefore actually invokes whisper's logic (toLowerCase() + "..."), and attempting to use whisper as imported either gives undefined or throws, since there was never a named export by that name to import. The fix is to match each import to its actual export style: import { shout } from ... for the named export, and import whisper from ... (or any name) for the default.

exercises.prompt: This code throws "SyntaxError: Only one default export allowed per module." Find the problem and fix it using named exports instead.
hints: How many default exports is a single module allowed to have?
config.js is trying to export two separate configuration objects, both as defaults -- that's structurally not possible.
Named exports don't have this one-per-module limit -- can you give each object its own fixed name instead?
exercises.solutionExplanation: A module can have at most one export default -- config.js tries to declare two, which is a SyntaxError caught before the module even runs, not a runtime error. Since there are genuinely two separate, equally-important values to expose here, named exports are the right tool: each configuration object gets its own fixed, exported name (retryConfig, timeoutConfig), and app.js imports both by name inside curly braces. This also sidesteps the ambiguity a single combined default export object would have introduced, where callers would need to know to write settings.retries and settings.timeout rather than getting each value directly.

assessments.prompt: Why do many style guides prefer named exports over default exports for most modules?
options: Named exports run faster at import time than default exports.
Default exports are not supported in Node.js, only in browsers.

Named exports have a fixed name enforced at every import site, which lets tooling reliably track and rename usages across a codebase; default exports let each importer choose any local name, breaking that guarantee.
A module can only have one named export, so named exports are simpler to reason about.
assessments.explanation: The practical reason is refactor safety: a named export's name is fixed, so every import of it must match (or explicitly alias), which lets an editor's rename tool or a find-all-references search reliably catch every usage. A default export can be imported under any local name the importer chooses, so two files importing the 'same' default export might call it two different things, with nothing to mechanically connect them. Performance (option A) isn't a real factor here. Option B is false -- default exports work identically in Node and browsers. Option D has the limit backwards -- it's default exports that are capped at one per module, not named exports.

assessments.prompt: Explain why declaring `const cache = {}` at the top of one module file doesn't create a global variable accessible from other files, and contrast this with how top-level variables worked in plain <script>-tag JavaScript.
assessments.modelAnswer: Each module -- each file using import/export syntax -- gets its own private top-level scope, separate from every other module's top-level scope. A const declared at the top level of one file lives only in that file's own module scope; it is never automatically visible anywhere else, no matter how many other files are loaded into the same page or program. The only way another file can see it at all is if the original module explicitly exports it (export const cache = {}) and the other file explicitly imports it (import { cache } from "./thatFile.js"). This is a deliberate design change from the older plain-<script>-tag model of loading JavaScript, where every script tag loaded onto a page shared exactly one global scope -- a top-level var or function declared in one script file became directly visible (and could be silently overwritten) by any other script file loaded on the same page, purely based on load order, with no explicit opt-in or connection between the files required. Module scope removes that entire category of accidental cross-file collision: nothing leaks between files unless a developer deliberately exports and imports it, which makes large codebases with many files dramatically safer to reason about.

concepts.title: The DOM and Events
concepts.description: The DOM is a live, mutable tree of objects representing the current page -- not the original HTML text -- and querySelector, addEventListener, and event bubbling are the manual tools React's JSX and synthetic event system exist to abstract away.
learningObjectives: Explain that the DOM is a live tree of objects representing the current page, distinct from the original HTML source text.
Select and mutate elements directly using querySelector and standard DOM properties.
Attach event listeners with addEventListener and explain why removeEventListener requires the same function reference.
Explain event bubbling at a conceptual level and predict the order handlers fire in a nested click.
Explain what React's JSX and synthetic event system abstract away, and why that context makes React's behavior less 'magic.'

sections.heading: The DOM Is a Live Tree of Objects
sections.body: The **DOM** (Document Object Model) is the browser's in-memory representation of the current page: a tree of JavaScript objects (`Node`s -- elements, text, comments), each with properties and methods, mirroring the nested structure of the HTML. The crucial thing to internalize: **the DOM is not the HTML source text** -- it's a live, mutable data structure that the browser builds by parsing that text once, and which JavaScript can then read and change directly, with the visible page updating immediately to match. If you view a page's 'source' (the raw HTML the server sent) versus inspecting it with browser DevTools' Elements panel (the live DOM) after some JavaScript has run, they can look completely different -- DevTools shows you the DOM as it exists *right now*, including anything JavaScript has added, removed, or changed since the page loaded, while 'view source' only ever shows the original, unmodified text. Every `document.createElement`, every `.textContent = ...` assignment, every `.appendChild(...)` call is directly mutating this live tree, not editing some underlying text file.

sections.heading: Selecting and Mutating Elements
sections.body: `document.querySelector(cssSelector)` returns the first element matching a CSS selector (`document.querySelector("#submit-btn")`, `document.querySelector(".card.active")`), or `null` if nothing matches; `document.querySelectorAll(cssSelector)` returns all matches as a `NodeList`. Once you have a reference to a real element, you mutate it directly through its properties: `el.textContent = "Updated"` sets its text safely; `el.classList.add("active")` / `.remove(...)` / `.toggle(...)` manage CSS classes without you having to manually parse or rebuild a class string; `el.style.color = "red"` sets an inline style. One safety note worth flagging: `el.innerHTML = someString` parses `someString` as raw HTML and inserts it, which means if `someString` ever contains unsanitized user input, you've opened a cross-site-scripting (XSS) vulnerability -- injected `<script>` or event-handler attributes in that string can execute. `el.textContent = someString` is the safe alternative when you just want to display text, since it's always treated as plain text, never parsed as markup.

sections.heading: Attaching Event Listeners
sections.body: `el.addEventListener("click", handlerFunction)` registers `handlerFunction` to run whenever a `click` event fires on `el`. Unlike the old single-slot `el.onclick = fn` approach, `addEventListener` lets you attach **multiple independent listeners** for the same event type to the same element -- all of them run, in the order they were added. To remove one later, `el.removeEventListener("click", handlerFunction)` requires passing **the exact same function reference** that was originally added -- calling `removeEventListener` with a new, separately-written arrow function or anonymous function, even one with identical-looking code, does not remove anything, because from `removeEventListener`'s point of view, it's a completely different function value that was never registered in the first place. This is why code that needs to later remove a listener typically stores the handler in a named variable or constant first, rather than passing an inline anonymous function straight into `addEventListener`.

sections.heading: Event Bubbling
sections.body: When an event fires on an element, it doesn't just run listeners attached directly to that element -- by default, it then **bubbles up** through that element's ancestors, running any matching listeners attached to each of them in turn, all the way up to `document`. Clicking a button nested inside several `<div>`s fires the button's own click listener first, then the immediately enclosing div's click listener (if one exists), then that div's parent's, and so on outward. This conceptual model -- events propagate outward through the DOM tree after firing on their original target -- is what makes **event delegation** possible: rather than attaching a separate listener to every single item in a long list, you can attach one listener to the list's parent container and inspect `event.target` (the actual element that was clicked) inside it, letting bubbling deliver every child click to that one listener. It's also why `event.stopPropagation()` exists -- to deliberately stop an event from continuing to bubble further up past the point where it's called, when a handler wants to be the last one to react to a given event.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for React
sections.body: React abstracts almost all of the above away, and understanding what's underneath is exactly what turns React's version of it from something that feels like unexplainable magic into something that just makes sense. You never call `document.createElement` or `.appendChild` yourself in React code -- JSX (covered in the React Fundamentals module) compiles to element descriptions that React turns into real DOM nodes for you, using the exact same underlying DOM APIs covered here, just automated. You don't typically call `addEventListener` directly either -- writing `<button onClick={handleClick}>` in JSX is React's declarative equivalent, wired up through React's own **synthetic event system**, a layer React builds on top of real DOM events to normalize inconsistencies across browsers and to batch multiple state updates together efficiently. And synthetic events still fundamentally bubble the same conceptual way real DOM events do -- a `stopPropagation()` call on a React synthetic event stops it from reaching a React `onClick` on a parent component, for the same underlying reason a real event listener's `stopPropagation()` does. None of this is a different mental model from what's covered in this concept; it's the same tree, the same events, the same bubbling, wrapped in a more declarative API.

examples.title: Selecting, Mutating, and Listening
examples.explanation: querySelector finds the real, live button element on the page -- the same object the browser is using to render what's currently on screen, not a copy or a description of it. Each click mutates that element directly: textContent updates the visible label immediately, and classList.toggle flips the active class on or off, which the page's CSS presumably uses to change the button's appearance. handleClick is stored in a named function so that a later removeEventListener call can reference the identical function value; passing a freshly-written function expression to removeEventListener, even one with identical-looking code, would silently fail to remove anything, since it wouldn't match the reference addEventListener originally stored.

examples.title: Event Bubbling Order
examples.explanation: Clicking the button fires the click event on the button first, since that's the actual target of the click -- "button" logs first. The event then bubbles outward through the DOM tree, next reaching #inner (the button's immediate parent), logging "inner", and finally reaching #outer, logging "outer" last. No listener here calls stopPropagation(), so the event is free to keep bubbling all the way up through every ancestor that has a matching listener, firing each one in strict inside-to-outside order.

misconceptions.description: The DOM is just the HTML source code, so inspecting an element in DevTools shows you exactly what's in the original HTML file.
misconceptions.clarification: The DOM is a live, in-memory tree of objects that the browser builds by parsing the HTML once, and JavaScript can then freely read and mutate that tree directly -- the visible page always reflects the DOM's current state, not the original source text. DevTools' Elements panel shows the DOM as it exists right now, including any changes JavaScript has made since the page loaded; 'view page source' shows only the original, unmodified HTML the server actually sent. After enough JavaScript has run, the two can look completely different from each other.

misconceptions.description: Calling el.removeEventListener("click", function() { ... }) removes a listener as long as the function's code looks the same as what was originally passed to addEventListener.
misconceptions.clarification: removeEventListener only removes a listener if it's given the exact same function reference that was originally passed to addEventListener -- it compares by identity, not by what the function's code does or looks like. Two separately written functions with identical bodies are still two different function values in memory, so passing a freshly-written one to removeEventListener silently does nothing (no error, the old listener just stays attached). To be able to remove a listener later, store the handler in a named variable/constant and pass that same reference to both addEventListener and removeEventListener.

exercises.prompt:
Given `
New
`, and this code, what gets logged, in what order, when the user clicks directly on the badge span?
exercises.code:
document.querySelector("#card").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("card clicked"));
document.querySelector("#badge").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("badge clicked"));
hints: The click's actual target is the badge, since that's the specific element the user clicked on -- which listener fires for that first?
After firing on its target, an event doesn't just stop there by default -- what does it do next, and in which direction through the tree?
card is badge's parent element -- does the event reach card's listener before or after badge's?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "badge clicked" logs first, then "card clicked" logs second -- the event fires on its actual target (badge) first, then bubbles upward to the parent (card).
exercises.solutionExplanation: The click event always fires on its actual target first -- the specific element the user clicked, which is #badge here -- so "badge clicked" is guaranteed to log first. By default, after firing on the target, the event bubbles upward through each ancestor in the DOM tree, and #card is badge's direct parent, so card's click listener fires next, logging "card clicked" second. Neither listener calls stopPropagation(), so nothing interrupts this normal bubbling sequence.

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to let the user toggle a highlight on and off by clicking a button repeatedly, and later remove that ability entirely by calling disableHighlighting(). But calling disableHighlighting() never actually removes the click behavior. Find and fix the bug.
hints: removeEventListener needs to be given the exact same function reference that addEventListener originally received -- not just similar-looking code.
Each of these two functions writes its own separate anonymous function() {...} -- are those two function expressions actually the same value in memory?
Try storing the handler in a named variable once, outside both functions, and passing that one reference to both addEventListener and removeEventListener.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code writes two separate anonymous function expressions -- one inside enableHighlighting, one inside disableHighlighting -- and even though their code looks identical, they are two entirely different function values in memory. removeEventListener compares by reference, not by code content, so passing a function that was never the one actually registered does nothing at all, silently. The fix pulls the handler out into its own named function, toggleHighlight, declared once; both enableHighlighting and disableHighlighting now reference that same single function value, so removeEventListener can correctly find and remove the listener that addEventListener originally added.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the DOM and the original HTML sent by the server?
options: The DOM and the original HTML source are always identical -- inspecting either one shows the same content.

The DOM is a live, mutable tree of objects built by parsing the HTML once; JavaScript can change the DOM directly, and the visible page reflects those changes without altering the original source text.
The DOM only updates when the page is reloaded from the server.
innerHTML and textContent behave identically, since both just set an element's HTML content.
assessments.explanation: The DOM starts as a tree built by parsing the original HTML, but from that point on it's an independent, live, in-memory structure -- JavaScript mutations to it (adding elements, changing text, updating attributes) take effect immediately on the visible page and do not touch or require re-fetching the original source. Option A is false the moment any JavaScript runs and changes something. Option C is false -- DOM updates happen immediately via script, with no reload needed. Option D is false and specifically dangerous to believe -- innerHTML parses its argument as HTML markup (a real XSS risk with untrusted input), while textContent always treats its argument as plain, unparsed text.

assessments.prompt: A developer who has only used React is confused by a bug involving addEventListener and asks why React never made them think about event bubbling before. Explain what React normally abstracts away here, and why understanding real DOM events still matters.
assessments.modelAnswer: In plain JavaScript, you manually select real DOM elements (querySelector), manually attach listeners to them (addEventListener), and those events bubble upward through the actual DOM tree by default, which is the mechanism this whole concept covers. React abstracts almost every part of that away: JSX like <button onClick={handleClick}> compiles down to React internally creating and wiring up the DOM element and attaching the actual event handling for you, so you never call addEventListener yourself in typical React code. React also layers its own synthetic event system on top of native browser events, mainly to smooth out cross-browser inconsistencies and to let React batch multiple resulting state updates efficiently, so what a React onClick handler receives (event) is a React-managed wrapper object, not literally the same object a raw addEventListener callback would receive. The reason understanding native bubbling still matters: React's synthetic events still conceptually bubble the same way real DOM events do -- a stopPropagation() call inside a React onClick can stop that click from also triggering a parent component's onClick, for essentially the same underlying reason a real addEventListener's stopPropagation() would. Debugging a case where a click handler on a nested element seems to also fire something on a parent, or figuring out why event delegation works the way it does in a component tree, both come back to the same bubbling model covered here -- React didn't replace that model, it just wrapped it in a more declarative API, so the underlying mental model is directly transferable rather than being separate 'React knowledge.'

concepts.title: Promises and async/await
concepts.description: A Promise represents an eventual result that settles exactly once, async/await is syntactic sugar for working with promises using ordinary-looking synchronous code, and awaiting inside a loop is one of the most common performance mistakes in real-world async code.
learningObjectives: Explain the readability and error-handling problems nested callbacks caused, and how promises address them.
Name a Promise's three states and explain what it means for a promise to settle exactly once.
Chain .then()/.catch() correctly and predict how errors propagate through a chain.
Explain that an async function always returns a promise, even when its body returns a plain value.
Identify when awaiting inside a loop unnecessarily serializes independent async work, and fix it with Promise.all.

sections.heading: The Callback Problem
A Promise's Three States
sections.body: A **Promise** is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. Every promise is in exactly one of three states at any given moment: **pending** (the operation hasn't finished yet -- the initial state for every promise), **fulfilled** (the operation completed successfully, and the promise now holds a resulting value), or **rejected** (the operation failed, and the promise now holds a reason/error). The critical rule: a **promise settles exactly once**. Once a promise moves from pending to either fulfilled or rejected, it is permanently locked into that state and that resulting value/reason forever -- it can never later change state, resolve a second time with a different value, or flip from fulfilled to rejected or back. This is precisely why a promise is not a good model for something that changes repeatedly over time (like a stream of events) -- it's a model for a single, one-time eventual outcome, settled once and done.

sections.heading: .then() and .catch() Chaining
sections.body:
`.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` registers callbacks to run once a promise settles; `.catch(onRejected)` is shorthand for `.then(undefined, onRejected)`. The feature that actually solves the nesting problem: **`.then()` always returns a new promise**, so calls can be chained one after another instead of nested inside each other:

```javascript
getUser(userId)
  .then(user => getPosts(user.id))
  .then(posts => getComments(posts[0].id))
  .then(comments => console.log(comments))
  .catch(err => console.error("Something failed:", err));
```

If any `.then()` callback returns a plain value, the next `.then()` in the chain receives that value directly. If a `.then()` callback instead returns *another promise* (as `getPosts(user.id)` does above), the chain automatically waits for that inner promise to settle and 'flattens' it -- the next `.then()` still just receives the eventual plain value, not a promise-wrapping-a-promise. And critically, a single `.catch()` at the end of the chain catches a rejection or a thrown error from **any** step earlier in the chain -- one shared error handler for the whole sequence, which is the direct fix for callback hell's duplicated error handling.

sections.heading: async/await as Sugar Over Promises
The Await-in-a-Loop Pitfall

examples.title: The Same Sequential Task: Callbacks vs Promises vs async/await
examples.explanation: All three versions do the exact same underlying work in the exact same order -- fetch a user, then fetch that user's posts, then log them -- and all three are ultimately built on promises somewhere (even the callback version could be wrapping promise-based APIs internally). The callback version nests one level deeper per step and needs handleError passed in separately at each level. The promise chain flattens the nesting into a linear .then() sequence with one shared .catch() at the end. The async/await version reads the most like ordinary synchronous code -- each await just looks like 'wait here, then continue with the value' -- with one try/catch covering every awaited step, exactly mirroring how you'd structure error handling for synchronous code.

examples.title: async Functions Always Return a Promise
examples.explanation: double is declared async, so calling it never gives you back x * 2 directly -- it always gives you a promise, which JavaScript automatically wraps the returned value (10) into as a fulfilled promise. console.log(result) shows the promise object itself, mid-flight or already settled, not the number. Getting the actual 10 back out requires unwrapping that promise, either with .then() (useful outside any async function) or with await from inside another async function -- both are just two different syntaxes for the same underlying 'wait for this promise, then hand me its value' operation.

examples.title: await-in-a-Loop vs Promise.all
examples.explanation: loadSequential's for loop awaits each fetchUser call before the loop even proceeds to the next id, so the three requests happen strictly back-to-back -- roughly 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 seconds total, even though none of the three fetches depends on any other's result. loadConcurrent calls fetchUser for every id first, with no awaiting in between, so all three network requests are already in flight simultaneously by the time Promise.all is reached; Promise.all then waits for whichever one takes longest, so the whole operation takes roughly as long as the single slowest fetch -- about 1 second, not 3. The results array from Promise.all preserves the original ids order regardless of which fetch actually finishes first.

misconceptions.description: await pauses all of JavaScript, blocking the entire page/program until the promise resolves.
misconceptions.clarification: await only pauses the execution of the specific async function it appears inside -- it does not block the JavaScript engine's event loop or any other code. While one async function is paused at an await, other functions, other event handlers, and other already-scheduled work continue running normally. This is exactly why await never freezes a page's UI the way a genuinely blocking, long-running synchronous loop would.

misconceptions.description: An async function that does `return 5;` returns the plain number 5, since that's literally what the return statement says.
misconceptions.clarification: Every async function always returns a Promise, no matter what its return statement returns -- the returned value is automatically wrapped in a fulfilled promise. return 5; inside an async function actually produces a promise that will fulfill with the value 5, not the number 5 itself. Getting the plain 5 back out always requires unwrapping that promise, either via await (from inside another async function) or .then().

misconceptions.description: A promise can be resolved more than once, or you can .then() it repeatedly to get a fresh, updated value each time, similar to how an event listener fires repeatedly.
misconceptions.clarification: A promise settles exactly once -- it transitions from pending to either fulfilled or rejected a single time, permanently, and calling resolve or reject again afterward has no effect at all. Any number of .then() callbacks, registered before or after the promise has already settled, all eventually receive that same one final settled value (or none, if the promise never settles). A promise models a single eventual outcome, not a repeating stream of values -- for genuinely repeating async events, you'd reach for something else, like an event listener or an observable/stream, not a promise.

exercises.prompt: What is the exact order these four lines log in?
hints: Everything before the first await inside an async function runs synchronously and immediately, the moment the function is called -- it doesn't wait for anything yet.
The line right after foo() is called -- console.log("D") -- is ordinary synchronous code sitting in the main flow of the script. Does it have to wait for foo to fully finish before it can run?

await always yields control back to the rest of the program at least once, even when awaiting something that's already resolved (like null) -- the code after await resumes only once everything already queued in the main synchronous flow has finished.
exercises.expectedAnswer: A, B, D, C -- foo() runs synchronously up through console.log("B") and then the await, at which point it pauses and control returns to the main script, which logs D; only after the main synchronous code finishes does execution return to resume foo() after its await, logging C last.
exercises.solutionExplanation: console.log("A") runs first, as ordinary top-level code. Calling foo() then runs synchronously up until it hits an await -- so console.log("B") runs immediately as part of that same call, before foo() returns anything back to the calling code. At the await null line, foo pauses and hands control back to whatever called it, without waiting for anything meaningful (null is not even a real pending promise) -- but await always defers its continuation to at least the next microtask, never resuming in the same synchronous pass. So execution returns to the line right after foo(), which is console.log("D"), and that runs next since it's plain synchronous code with nothing to wait for. Only once all currently-running synchronous code (including that D log) has finished does the JavaScript engine process the queued continuation of foo(), resuming after the await and finally logging "C" last. This A, B, D, C order is the single most common 'gotcha' interview-style question about async/await, precisely because await null looks like it should do nothing, but it still always yields at least one turn.

exercises.prompt: This function fetches profile data for five independent user IDs, but it's noticeably slower than expected -- each request seems to wait for the previous one. Find and fix the performance bug.
hints: fetchProfile(id) for one id doesn't depend on the result of fetchProfile for any other id -- these five requests are all independent of each other.
Inside the for loop, await pauses the loop itself before moving to the next iteration -- so no request even starts until the previous one has fully finished.
Try starting every fetchProfile call first (with .map, no await yet), and only then waiting for all of the resulting promises together.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original for loop awaits fetchProfile(id) on every iteration before moving on to the next id, which means each of the five requests waits for the previous one to completely finish before it even starts -- turning five independent, potentially-simultaneous requests into a strictly serial chain, roughly five times slower than necessary. The fix uses userIds.map(id => fetchProfile(id)) to call fetchProfile for every id immediately, back to back with no awaiting in between, so all five requests are already in flight over the network before the function does any waiting at all. await Promise.all(promises) then waits for all of them together, resolving once the slowest one finishes, and returns an array of every result in the same order as userIds -- roughly as fast as the single slowest request, rather than the sum of all five.

exercises.prompt: Given an already-implemented function `fetchUser(id)` that returns a promise resolving to a user object, write an async function `loadUsersConcurrently(ids)` that fetches all of the given ids' users concurrently (not one at a time) and returns a promise resolving to an array of the user objects, in the same order as ids. If any individual fetch fails, the whole function should reject with that error.
hints: Kick off every fetchUser call first, with no await yet, so all the requests start at roughly the same time.
.map over ids to get back an array of promises -- one call per id, none of them awaited individually inside the loop.

Promise.all takes an array of promises and gives you back one promise that resolves with an array of all their results, in the same order -- and it naturally rejects if any one of them rejects, which matches the required behavior here.
exercises.solutionExplanation: ids.map(id => fetchUser(id)) calls fetchUser once per id, immediately and with no awaiting in between, so every request starts essentially at the same time rather than one after another -- this is the concurrency requirement satisfied. Promise.all(promises) takes that array of in-flight promises and returns a single new promise that resolves once every one of them has resolved, with its resolved value being an array of all their individual results, in the same order the promises were given (regardless of which one actually finishes first) -- satisfying the 'same order as ids' requirement. Promise.all also automatically rejects as soon as any single promise in the array rejects, which is exactly the 'reject with that error if any fetch fails' behavior asked for, with no extra code needed to wire that up.

options: "Amara"
undefined
A Promise object (which will fulfill with the value "Amara")
A SyntaxError, since async functions can't return plain strings
assessments.explanation: Every async function always returns a promise, regardless of what its return statement returns -- the returned value "Amara" is automatically wrapped into a promise that fulfills with that value. Calling getName() without awaiting or .then()-ing it just gives you that promise object itself, not the eventual string. Getting "Amara" back out requires either await getName() inside another async function, or getName().then(name => ...). There's nothing wrong with returning a plain string from an async function -- it's extremely common -- it's just always implicitly wrapped.

assessments.prompt: A colleague's code fetches five independent pieces of data using five separate awaited calls inside a for loop, and complains that the page feels sluggish. Explain what's likely happening and how you'd fix it, including any caveat about the fix.
assessments.modelAnswer: The likely problem is exactly the await-in-a-loop pattern: if the loop awaits each async call before moving to the next iteration, the five requests -- even though none of them depends on any other's result -- end up running strictly one after another rather than at the same time. If each request takes, say, half a second, that's roughly two and a half seconds total instead of roughly half a second if they'd run concurrently, which lines up with a 'sluggish' complaint. The fix is to stop awaiting inside the loop and instead start every request immediately (commonly via .map(id => someAsyncCall(id)), which calls the async function for every item with no awaiting yet, collecting the resulting promises into an array), then await Promise.all(thatArray) once, outside the loop, to wait for all five to finish together. The one caveat worth raising back to the colleague: Promise.all rejects as soon as any single one of the five requests fails, discarding the results of any that had already succeeded -- so if the use case genuinely needs to know the outcome of every request regardless of individual failures (e.g., 'show me whichever of these five succeeded, and separately flag which ones failed'), Promise.allSettled is the more appropriate tool, since it always resolves with a per-item status rather than rejecting the whole batch on the first failure.

concepts.title: fetch and Error Handling
concepts.description: The fetch API's promise resolves for any completed HTTP response -- including 404s and 500s -- and rejects only on network-level failure, so you must explicitly check response.ok yourself, a genuinely common misconception that leads to silently-swallowed errors.
learningObjectives: Describe the basic shape of a fetch call, including the separate step needed to read the response body.
Explain that fetch's promise rejects only on network failure, not on HTTP error status codes, and check response.ok/response.status accordingly.
Write a fetch call wrapped in try/catch using async/await that correctly handles both network failures and HTTP error responses.
Explain how the loading/success/error pattern shown here maps onto how React data-fetching hooks are typically built.

sections.heading: The fetch API's Basic Shape
fetch Does Not Throw on HTTP Error Status Codes
sections.body:
This is the single most common, and most consequential, misconception about `fetch`: **`fetch`'s promise does not reject just because the server responded with an error status like 404 or 500.** As far as `fetch` is concerned, a 404 Not Found is a *successfully completed HTTP exchange* -- the server responded, the browser got a full response, nothing about the network transport failed -- so the promise **resolves** normally, with a `Response` object whose `.status` happens to be `404`. `fetch`'s promise only **rejects** for genuine network-level failures: DNS resolution failure, no connectivity at all, a CORS policy blocking the request, the connection being dropped mid-flight.

This means code like `fetch(url).then(res => res.json()).catch(err => handleError(err))` will happily proceed past `.then()` and never reach `.catch()` even when the server returns a 500 with an error body -- it'll just hand you the parsed error JSON as if it were a normal successful result, with nothing at all signaling that anything went wrong. You must check **`response.ok`** (a boolean, `true` for any status in the 200-299 range) or **`response.status`** directly yourself, and explicitly decide what 'failure' means for your case -- typically by throwing an error yourself when `response.ok` is `false`, so that your existing error-handling path (`.catch()` or `try`/`catch`) actually gets a chance to run.

sections.heading: try/catch with async/await
This Pattern Is What React Data-Fetching Hooks Are Built Around
sections.body: The three-state shape this concept has been building toward -- **loading** (the request is in flight), **success** (data arrived), **error** (something went wrong, whether network-level or an HTTP error status you explicitly detected) -- is exactly the model that React's data-fetching patterns are built on top of. A typical custom hook for fetching data (`useEffect` + a few `useState` calls, or a dedicated library like React Query/TanStack Query) is, underneath, running essentially the same `try`/`await fetch`/check-`response.ok`/`catch` logic shown here, and exposing its outcome as exactly those three states (`isLoading`, `data`, `error`) for a component to render conditionally. Understanding this plain-JavaScript version first is what makes those hooks' behavior predictable rather than opaque -- there's no different underlying mechanism happening inside them, just this same pattern, wrapped in React's state and lifecycle management.

examples.title: Basic fetch with async/await
examples.explanation: The first await waits for the HTTP response to arrive and gives back a Response object -- headers and status are available immediately at that point, but the body hasn't been read yet. The second await, on response.json(), waits for the body to be read and parsed as JSON, which is its own separate asynchronous step. This example deliberately omits error handling to isolate the basic two-step shape; the next example shows why that omission is dangerous.

examples.title: The Misconception in Action: A 404 That Never Reaches catch
examples.explanation: In the first version, fetch's promise resolves normally for the 404 response -- as far as fetch is concerned, the request completed successfully, it just happens to carry a 404 status. res.json() also resolves normally, parsing whatever error body the server sent (perhaps { error: "User not found" }), and that gets logged by the second .then() as if it were a legitimate successful result -- .catch() never runs, because nothing in this chain ever rejected. The fixed version adds an explicit res.ok check inside the first .then(), and throws an Error when it's false -- throwing inside a .then() callback causes the promise chain to reject from that point onward, which is what finally gives .catch() something to actually catch.

misconceptions.description: fetch automatically throws an error (or rejects its promise) whenever the server responds with an error status like 404 or 500.
misconceptions.clarification: fetch's promise only rejects for network-level failures -- no connectivity, DNS failure, a blocked CORS request, a dropped connection. A completed HTTP exchange that happens to carry a 404 or 500 status is, from fetch's point of view, still a successful request/response cycle, so the promise resolves normally with a Response object whose status/ok properties reflect the error. You must explicitly check response.ok (or response.status) and decide what counts as a failure for your use case, typically by throwing your own Error when it's not ok, so your catch block or .catch() actually gets triggered.

misconceptions.description: Once you have the Response object from fetch, you already have the actual data -- it's already been parsed and is ready to use.
misconceptions.clarification: The Response object gives you access to metadata (status, headers, ok) as soon as the response starts arriving, but reading and parsing the body is a distinct, separate asynchronous step -- response.json() (or .text(), .blob(), etc.), which itself returns another promise that needs its own await or .then(). This two-step design exists because a response body can be large or streamed and isn't eagerly loaded into memory just because the headers arrived; forgetting this second await is a common source of 'why is my data a pending promise' confusion.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to throw a clear error when a request fails, but callers report it never seems to notice failed requests -- it just returns whatever error data the server sent, without complaint. Find and fix the bug.
hints: await fetch(...) resolving without throwing doesn't mean the request 'succeeded' in the sense you probably care about -- what does fetch's promise actually reject for?
A 404 or 500 response is still a resolved promise from fetch's perspective -- you need to check something on the response object yourself to detect it.
response.ok is a boolean specifically meant for this check -- what should getProduct do when it's false?
exercises.solutionExplanation: await fetch(...) only throws for network-level failures, not for a completed request that happens to carry an error status -- so a 404 response resolves normally, and the original code proceeds straight to parsing and returning the (likely error-message) body as if it were legitimate data, with the try/catch never noticing anything went wrong. Adding if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(...) } explicitly turns 'the server said this request failed' into an actual thrown error, at the exact point where getProduct can already see the response's status -- from there, the surrounding try/catch (or an outer .catch()) works exactly as originally intended, because there's now something for it to actually catch.

exercises.prompt: Write an async function `getJson(url)` that: performs a GET fetch to url; throws a descriptive Error (including the HTTP status code in its message) if the response is not ok; otherwise returns the parsed JSON body. Network failures (fetch itself rejecting) should propagate naturally, with no special handling needed beyond that.
hints: Start with a plain await fetch(url) -- if the network itself fails, that line already throws on its own with no extra code needed.
Right after that, check response.ok, and if it's false, throw your own Error including response.status in the message somehow (a template literal is convenient for this).
Only after that check passes should you await response.json() and return its result.
exercises.solutionExplanation: await fetch(url) is left unwrapped in its own try/catch inside getJson deliberately -- if it rejects due to a genuine network failure, that rejection propagates naturally out of getJson (since getJson is itself async, an unhandled throw/rejection inside it becomes a rejection of the promise getJson returns), so the caller's own try/catch around getJson(...) still catches it, with no extra code needed inside getJson for that case. The explicit if (!response.ok) check is what handles the case fetch itself doesn't treat as a failure -- an HTTP error status -- by manually throwing a new Error with the status code included, which becomes the rejection reason for getJson's returned promise from that point on. Only once both failure modes are ruled out does the function proceed to await response.json() and return the parsed data.

assessments.prompt:
```javascript
const response = await fetch("/api/does-not-exist");
```
If the server responds with a 404 status, what happens on this line?
options: The fetch promise rejects, and this line throws.
The fetch promise resolves normally with a Response object whose status is 404 and whose ok property is false.
fetch automatically retries the request a few times before giving up.
response ends up as null.
assessments.explanation: fetch's promise only rejects for network-level failures (no connectivity, DNS issues, CORS blocks, a dropped connection) -- a 404 is a fully completed, successful HTTP exchange from fetch's point of view, so the promise resolves normally. The resulting Response object correctly reflects the failure through its own properties: status is 404, and ok (true only for 200-299) is false -- but the promise itself never rejected, which is exactly why response.ok must be checked explicitly rather than relying on a catch block to notice this kind of failure. fetch performs no automatic retries, and response is a real object, never null, once the promise resolves.

assessments.prompt: Explain how the loading/success/error pattern from manually handling fetch maps onto what a React data-fetching hook (like a custom useUser(id) hook, or a call to a library like React Query) is doing internally.
assessments.modelAnswer: Manually handling a fetch call well requires modeling three possible states over the request's lifetime: it's in flight and nothing is known yet (loading), it completed and you have usable data (success), or something went wrong -- either fetch itself rejected from a network failure, or you explicitly detected and threw for a bad HTTP status via response.ok (error). A hand-written async function using try/await fetch/check response.ok/catch is really just implementing that same three-state model as plain control flow, without persisting the intermediate 'loading' state anywhere a UI could observe it. A React data-fetching hook does the same underlying work -- fetch the URL, await the response, check its status, parse the body, handle failures -- but wraps each of those three states in its own piece of React state (commonly isLoading, data, and error, via useState, updated inside a useEffect that kicks off the fetch), so a component can read that state on every render and conditionally show a spinner, the actual data, or an error message. Libraries like React Query formalize and extend this exact pattern further (adding caching, retries, and background refetching on top), but the core three states and the same underlying fetch-and-check-response.ok logic are still there underneath -- understanding the plain-JavaScript version means none of that hook or library behavior needs to be taken on faith as 'how React does data fetching' -- it's the same mechanism, just wired into component state.

concepts.title: ES6+ Features
concepts.description: Template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing are modern syntax additions that each solve a specific, common pain point -- and the ?? vs || distinction in particular fixes a genuine bug class involving legitimate falsy values like 0.
learningObjectives: Use template literals for string interpolation and multi-line strings.
Use optional chaining (?.) to safely access possibly-missing nested properties without manual guard checks.
Explain the difference between ?? and ||, and predict when that difference produces a different result.
Situate template literals, optional chaining, nullish coalescing, arrow functions, and let/const as part of the same modern JavaScript syntax wave.

sections.heading: Template Literals
sections.body: **Template literals** use backticks (`` ` ``) instead of quotes, and support two features string concatenation never had: **interpolation** with `${expression}`, and genuine **multi-line strings**. Before template literals, building a string from variables meant concatenation: `"Hello, " + name + "! You have " + count + " messages."` -- readable enough for two variables, but it degrades fast as the number of interpolated values grows, since you're constantly breaking in and out of the string to add `+` operators. The same string as a template literal reads far more directly: `` `Hello, ${name}! You have ${count} messages.` `` -- the literal text and the dynamic parts are visually distinct without any `+` noise. `${ }` accepts any expression, not just a variable name -- `` `Total: ${price * quantity}` `` or `` `${isAdmin ? "Admin" : "User"}` `` both work directly inline. Template literals also span multiple lines with no special escape needed -- a literal newline inside the backticks is just part of the string -- where a plain string literal would require an explicit `\n` and string concatenation across lines entirely.

sections.heading: Optional Chaining (?.)
sections.body: Accessing a deeply nested property is risky if any link in the chain might be missing: `user.address.city` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` the moment `user.address` is `undefined` or `null`, not just when `user` itself is. The traditional defense was a chain of manual guards: `user && user.address && user.address.city`, which gets more unwieldy the deeper the chain goes. **Optional chaining**, `?.`, does the same job far more directly: `user?.address?.city` evaluates left to right, and the moment any `?.` finds its left-hand side to be `null` or `undefined`, it **short-circuits immediately**, returning `undefined` for the whole expression rather than throwing. It also works on method calls (`user.greet?.()` -- calls `greet` only if it exists, otherwise evaluates to `undefined` with no error) and on array/bracket access (`arr?.[0]`). One precision point worth being exact about: each `?.` only guards the specific step it's attached to -- `user?.address.city` (with only one `?.`) still throws if `user.address` itself turns out to be missing, because only the `user?.` step is protected; you need a `?.` at every step you actually want guarded, not just the first one.

sections.heading: Nullish Coalescing (??) and How It Differs From ||
Part of the Same ES6+ Wave
sections.body: Template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing aren't isolated tricks -- they're part of the same multi-year trend in JavaScript's evolution (starting with ES6/ES2015 and continuing through later yearly releases, collectively often called 'ES6+' informally) of adding more expressive, safer syntax for patterns developers were already writing by hand, just more verbosely and more error-pronely. `let`/`const` (covered in the closures/scope foundations) replaced `var`'s looser function-scoping with real block scope. Arrow functions (covered in the Functions concept) gave callbacks predictable `this` behavior. Destructuring and spread/rest (covered in their own concept) replaced manual property-by-property extraction and array/object copying. Optional chaining and nullish coalescing continue exactly that same throughline, just aimed specifically at the 'safely read something that might be missing' and 'provide a real default' problems. None of these features change what JavaScript is fundamentally capable of -- everything they do was always possible longhand -- they just make the common, correct way to write something shorter and harder to get subtly wrong.

examples.title: Template Literals vs Concatenation
examples.explanation: messageOld and messageNew produce the identical final string, but messageNew reads more directly -- the literal text and the two dynamic values are visually distinct without any + operators breaking up the flow. receipt demonstrates the multi-line capability: the literal newlines between backticks become real \n characters in the resulting string automatically, with no explicit escape sequence or string concatenation across separate lines required.

examples.title: Optional Chaining and Nullish Coalescing Together
examples.explanation: order.shipping?.trackingNumber safely returns undefined instead of throwing, since order.shipping itself doesn't exist -- the ?. short-circuits right there. order.customer?.phone is undefined (customer exists, but has no phone property), and ?? "No phone on file" correctly supplies a fallback since undefined is exactly what ?? triggers on. order.discount ?? 5 correctly returns the real value 0, since ?? only falls through on null/undefined, not on other falsy values. order.discount || 5 demonstrates the classic bug: 0 is falsy, so || treats it the same as if discount were missing entirely, incorrectly replacing a real, meaningful 0 with 5.

misconceptions.description: ?? and || are interchangeable ways to write 'use this value, or a default if it's not set' -- pick whichever you find more readable.
misconceptions.clarification: They trigger on different conditions: || falls through on any falsy value (0, "", false, NaN, null, undefined), while ?? falls through only on null or undefined specifically. Whenever the value in question has a legitimate falsy value that's still meaningful and should NOT be replaced -- a real 0 quantity, a deliberate false toggle, an intentionally empty string -- || silently replaces it with the fallback while ?? correctly preserves it. They only produce identical results when the value can never legitimately be anything other than null/undefined/truthy, which is not the common case for numbers, booleans, or strings.

misconceptions.description: Optional chaining (?.) means you never have to worry about a property-access error anywhere in that expression again.
misconceptions.clarification: Each ?. only guards the specific link it's attached to -- it doesn't retroactively protect every step in a chain. user?.address.city still throws if user.address itself is null/undefined, because only the user?. step is optional; you need a ?. at every step you actually want protected (user?.address?.city). Optional chaining also doesn't prevent every kind of error -- calling something with ?.() that exists but genuinely isn't a function still throws a TypeError; ?. specifically guards against the left-hand side being null/undefined, nothing more general than that.

exercises.prompt: What does each line print?
hints: ?? only cares whether the value is specifically null or undefined -- nothing else counts, no matter how 'empty' it looks.
|| cares about the full falsy list -- 0 and "" both qualify as falsy, even though they're both legitimate, intentional values here.
settings.timeout is explicitly null, not just missing -- does ?? treat that as 'nothing here, use the fallback' or as a real value to keep?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 0 (?? preserves the real 0), 5 (|| incorrectly replaces the real 0), "" (?? preserves the real empty string), "default label" (|| incorrectly replaces the real empty string), 1000 (?? correctly replaces null, since null is exactly what ?? triggers on).
exercises.solutionExplanation: settings.retries is 0, a legitimate falsy-but-meaningful value: ?? only replaces null/undefined, so it correctly returns 0; || replaces any falsy value, so it incorrectly returns the fallback 5 instead of the real 0. settings.label is "", the same situation: ?? correctly preserves the empty string, while || incorrectly treats it as missing and returns "default label". settings.timeout is explicitly null, which is exactly the condition ?? is designed to catch -- so ?? correctly falls through to the fallback 1000 here, unlike the previous two cases where falling through was the wrong behavior.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to safely display a user's city, or 'Unknown' if any part of the address chain is missing, but it still throws when address itself is missing. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Count the ?. marks in user?.address.city -- how many links in this chain are actually protected?
user?. protects against user itself being missing, but what protects the .city access if address turns out to be missing?
You need a ?. at every step you want guarded, not just the first one in the chain.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code only has one ?., after user -- that protects against user itself being null/undefined, but .address.city after it is written with plain dot notation, so if user.address turns out to be undefined (as it is for {}, which has no address property at all), accessing .city off of it still throws a TypeError, exactly as if no optional chaining were used at all for that step. Adding a second ?. -- user?.address?.city -- protects both links in the chain independently: if user is missing, the first ?. short-circuits to undefined immediately; if user exists but address is missing, the second ?. catches that and also short-circuits to undefined; either way, the overall expression becomes undefined rather than throwing, and ?? "Unknown" then supplies the intended fallback.

options: 0, correctly preserving the real value
10, because || treats 0 as falsy and replaces it with the fallback, incorrectly overriding a real, intentional 0% discount
undefined, because discountPercent doesn't exist on the object
A TypeError, because you can't use || with the number 0
assessments.explanation: 0 is one of the falsy values, so order.discountPercent || 10 treats a real, explicit 0 exactly the same as if discountPercent were missing or undefined -- it falls through to the fallback 10, incorrectly reporting a 10% discount when the actual intended value was 0%. This is precisely the bug class nullish coalescing (??) exists to fix: order.discountPercent ?? 10 would correctly return 0, since ?? only falls through on null or undefined, treating a real 0 as a value worth keeping rather than a signal that something is missing.

assessments.prompt: Explain why template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing are often grouped together as 'modern JavaScript features,' and what they have in common with arrow functions and let/const, despite all doing very different things syntactically.
assessments.modelAnswer: Each of these features solves a specific, narrow pain point that developers were already working around by hand, using more verbose and more error-prone patterns, before the feature existed. Template literals replace string concatenation's + chains with direct ${} interpolation and native multi-line support. Optional chaining replaces a manually-written chain of && guards (user && user.address && user.address.city) with a single, more direct ?. per step. Nullish coalescing replaces a common but subtly incorrect use of || as a default-value operator with one that only triggers on null/undefined, fixing a real bug class involving legitimate falsy values like 0 or an empty string. None of these are capabilities JavaScript lacked before -- everything they do was always achievable with older syntax -- they just make the correct, common version of that pattern shorter and much harder to get subtly wrong. This is exactly the same throughline as let/const (replacing var's confusing function-scoping and hoisting behavior with predictable block scope) and arrow functions (replacing manual .bind(this) or var self = this workarounds with lexical this by default): all of them are part of the same multi-year trend of the language absorbing common, error-prone hand-written patterns into safer, more direct built-in syntax, rather than any one of them being an isolated, unrelated trick.

concepts.title: npm and JSON
concepts.description: package.json is a project's manifest of dependencies and scripts, npm install and npm run are how you act on it, semantic versioning ranges control what gets installed, and JSON itself is the same plain-text data format you've already used from Python -- just with different language bindings.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of package.json as a project manifest, including dependencies, devDependencies, and scripts.
Explain what npm install does and why package-lock.json is committed to version control.
Run project scripts with npm run and explain the purpose of the scripts field.
Interpret ^ and ~ semantic versioning ranges and predict which versions each would allow.
Explain that JSON is a strict, language-independent data format, and connect it to JSON already seen in Python.

sections.heading: package.json: The Project Manifest
sections.body: **`package.json`** is the single file at the root of a JavaScript/Node project that describes it: its name and version, metadata like a description and license, and -- most practically important day to day -- its **dependencies**. `"dependencies"` lists packages the project needs to actually run in production (a UI library, a data-fetching helper); `"devDependencies"` lists packages only needed while developing (a test runner, a linter, a build tool) that don't need to ship with the finished application. Every one of these is recorded as a package name mapped to a version range (covered below). This file is effectively the project's single source of truth for 'what does this project depend on, and how do you build/run/test it' -- anyone who clones the project can read package.json and immediately know both.

sections.heading: npm install and Running Scripts
sections.body:
**`npm install`** (often just `npm i`) reads `package.json`'s dependencies and `devDependencies`, resolves a specific, compatible version for each one (and every dependency those dependencies themselves need, recursively), downloads them all into a `node_modules` folder, and writes (or updates) a **`package-lock.json`** file recording the *exact* version of every single package that was actually installed, down to the deepest nested dependency. That lockfile is what makes builds reproducible: without it, two different developers (or a developer's machine versus a CI server) running `npm install` against the same `package.json` at different times could resolve slightly different versions if anything in the dependency tree published an update in between -- `package-lock.json` pins the exact tree that was actually resolved, so everyone gets the identical set of versions. This is exactly why `package-lock.json` is committed to version control, while `node_modules` itself almost always is not (it's fully regenerable from the lockfile, and it's typically enormous).

The `"scripts"` field in `package.json` maps short names to actual shell commands: `"scripts": { "dev": "vite", "test": "jest", "build": "vite build" }`. Running `npm run dev` executes whatever command is mapped to `"dev"`. (`start` and `test` get a small shortcut -- `npm start` and `npm test` work without the word `run` -- everything else needs the full `npm run <name>`.) This exists so a team doesn't need to memorize or agree on raw tool invocations individually -- everyone just runs `npm run build`, regardless of what specific tool or flags that maps to underneath, and that mapping can change over time without anyone needing to change their own habits.

sections.heading: Semantic Versioning: ^ and ~
sections.body: Package versions generally follow **semantic versioning** (semver): `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, e.g. `4.17.21` -- `MAJOR` increments for breaking changes, `MINOR` for new backward-compatible features, `PATCH` for backward-compatible bug fixes. The prefix in front of a version range in `package.json` controls how much of an automatic upgrade `npm install` is allowed to pick: **`^4.17.21`** (caret, the default npm writes) allows any version that doesn't change the leftmost non-zero number -- so it can install up to (but not including) `5.0.0`, meaning any `MINOR` or `PATCH` update is fine, but no `MAJOR` bump. **`~4.17.21`** (tilde) is more conservative -- it only allows `PATCH`-level updates, up to (but not including) `4.18.0`. An exact version with no prefix at all (`4.17.21`) allows no automatic updates whatsoever. Concretely: with `"lodash": "^4.17.21"` in `package.json`, if `4.17.25` and `5.0.0` both exist, a fresh `npm install` picks `4.17.25` (a minor/patch update, allowed) and never `5.0.0` (a major bump, not allowed by `^`). With `~4.17.21` instead, only patch-level releases like `4.17.25` are allowed -- a hypothetical `4.18.0` (a minor bump) would not be, even though `^` would have allowed it.

sections.heading: JSON as a Data Interchange Format
sections.body:
`package.json` is itself written in **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation), but JSON is not JavaScript-specific despite the name and despite looking almost like a JavaScript object literal -- it's a plain-text data format with its own strict rules, used constantly for things entirely unrelated to JavaScript: API responses, configuration files, data exports, and yes, `package.json` itself. JSON supports exactly: objects (`{ }`), arrays (`[ ]`), strings (always double-quoted), numbers, `true`/`false`, and `null` -- nothing else. Critically, it is **stricter** than a JavaScript object literal: JSON requires every key to be a double-quoted string (unquoted or single-quoted keys are invalid JSON, even though they're valid in an actual JS object literal), it has no comments, no trailing commas, and no way to represent a function, `undefined`, or a `Symbol` at all.

If you've studied Python in this same app, you've already used exactly this format there too -- `json.loads()`/`json.dumps()` read and write the identical JSON text format, with the identical rules; JavaScript's equivalents are `JSON.parse()` (text to a JS value) and `JSON.stringify()` (a JS value to text). Same format, same on-the-wire rules, entirely different language on either side reading or writing it -- which is exactly the point of JSON existing as a format in the first place: it's meant to be a neutral, language-independent way for systems written in different languages to exchange structured data without either side needing to know or care what language produced or will consume it.

examples.title: A Minimal package.json
examples.explanation: react and react-dom sit under dependencies because the built application actually needs them at runtime in the browser. vite (the build tool) and jest (the test runner) sit under devDependencies because they're only needed while developing and building the project -- the finished, shipped app doesn't need either of them present to run. npm run dev executes vite (the command mapped to the "dev" script name); npm test works without the word run, since test is one of the two special-cased script names npm recognizes directly.

examples.title: ^ vs ~ With Concrete Available Versions
examples.explanation: ^1.4.0 allows any update that keeps the leftmost non-zero version number (1, the MAJOR version) unchanged -- so both the PATCH bump to 1.4.5 and the MINOR bump to 1.6.0 are allowed, and npm picks the highest one available, 1.6.0; the MAJOR bump to 2.0.0 is excluded since ^ never crosses that boundary. ~1.4.0 is more restrictive -- it only allows PATCH-level updates within the same MINOR version (1.4.x), so 1.4.5 is allowed but 1.6.0 (a MINOR bump, from 1.4 to 1.6) is not; npm picks 1.4.5 as the highest version satisfying that narrower range.

misconceptions.description: JSON and a JavaScript object literal are exactly the same thing, so it's fine to add comments or use single-quoted/unquoted keys in a .json file.
misconceptions.clarification: JSON is a stricter subset of what a JavaScript object literal can express, even though the two look very similar. Valid JSON requires every key and every string value to be wrapped in double quotes specifically (not single quotes, and keys can never be left unquoted), allows no comments anywhere, and allows no trailing comma after the last item in an object or array. A JavaScript object literal permits all of those things (unquoted keys, single quotes, trailing commas, and of course actual JS comments), but a real .json file -- and anything passed through JSON.parse -- does not; a JSON parser will throw a syntax error on any of them.

misconceptions.description: ^1.2.3 and ~1.2.3 mean roughly the same thing -- both just mean 'approximately this version, updates are fine.'
misconceptions.clarification: They allow meaningfully different ranges of automatic updates. ^1.2.3 allows any MINOR or PATCH update, up to (but not including) the next MAJOR version -- so it would accept an update to 1.9.0. ~1.2.3 only allows PATCH-level updates within the same MINOR version -- it would accept 1.2.9 but not 1.3.0. Given the same set of available published versions, ^ and ~ can genuinely resolve to different actual installed versions, which matters when a MINOR release happens to introduce a bug or a subtle behavior change you'd rather not pick up automatically.

exercises.prompt: A package.json has `"chart-lib": "~2.3.0"`. The published versions available on the registry are 2.3.0, 2.3.4, 2.4.0, and 3.0.0. Which version does a fresh `npm install` pick, and why?
hints: ~ only allows updates within the same MINOR version number -- here, that means staying within the 2.3.x line.
2.4.0 changes the MINOR number (2.3 to 2.4) -- does ~ allow crossing that boundary?
Among the versions that ARE allowed, npm always picks the highest one available, not just any matching one.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 2.3.4 -- the highest version that stays within the same MINOR line (2.3.x) as the range specifies; 2.4.0 and 3.0.0 are both excluded because ~ only allows PATCH-level updates.
exercises.solutionExplanation: ~2.3.0 permits only PATCH-level updates while keeping MAJOR.MINOR fixed at 2.3 -- so any version of the form 2.3.x is allowed, but 2.4.0 (a MINOR bump) and 3.0.0 (a MAJOR bump) are both outside the allowed range. Among the available versions, 2.3.0 and 2.3.4 both satisfy 2.3.x, and npm always resolves to the highest satisfying version it can find, so it picks 2.3.4.

exercises.prompt: This file is meant to be a valid config.json, but a JSON.parse() call on its contents throws a SyntaxError. Find every problem preventing it from being valid JSON and rewrite it correctly.
hints: JSON requires every key to be wrapped in double quotes -- is name written that way here?
Single-quoted strings aren't valid JSON at all, even though they're valid JavaScript -- what does 'weather-app' need to become?
Look for two more problems: something JSON has no syntax for at all (hint: it's a line explaining what timeout means), and something left over after the very last property that JSON doesn't allow.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Four separate problems, all common when someone writes JSON as if it were a JS object literal: name was an unquoted key (JSON requires every key double-quoted); 'weather-app' used single quotes (JSON strings must be double-quoted, no exceptions); the // comment line has no equivalent in JSON at all -- JSON has zero comment syntax, and a parser will fail on it, not skip over it; and the trailing comma after "retries": 3 is invalid, since JSON does not allow a comma after the last property in an object (or the last element in an array). The corrected version fixes all four: name and its value are properly double-quoted, the comment is removed entirely, and the trailing comma after the last property is deleted.

assessments.prompt: A package.json lists `"some-lib": "^2.5.0"`. Which of the following newly published versions would npm install be allowed to pick?
assessments.explanation: ^2.5.0 allows any MINOR or PATCH update that keeps the leftmost non-zero number -- the MAJOR version, 2 -- unchanged, so anything from 2.5.0 up to (but not including) 3.0.0 is allowed. 2.9.1 fits that range (still MAJOR version 2). 3.0.0 is excluded because it's a MAJOR bump, exactly what ^ refuses to cross. 1.9.9 is an older MAJOR version, not a valid upgrade target at all. 2.4.9 is actually older than the specified 2.5.0 minimum, so it wouldn't be selected either -- npm install only moves forward from the specified version within the allowed range.

assessments.prompt: Someone who has only used Python's json module asks whether JavaScript's JSON.parse/JSON.stringify are 'basically the same idea.' Explain how JSON as a format relates to the two languages.
assessments.modelAnswer: JSON is not tied to either language -- it's a plain-text data format with its own fixed, strict grammar (objects, arrays, double-quoted strings, numbers, true/false, null, and nothing beyond that), designed specifically so that programs written in completely different languages can exchange structured data without either side needing to know what language the other one is written in. Python's json.loads() and JavaScript's JSON.parse() both do the identical job: take that same plain text format and turn it into that language's native in-memory data structures (a Python dict/list, or a JS object/array) -- and json.dumps() and JSON.stringify() do the reverse, turning native data back into that same shared text format. So yes, they're 'basically the same idea' in the strongest possible sense: it's not just a similar idea implemented twice, it's the exact same wire format and the exact same rules, with each language providing its own pair of functions to read and write it. The one thing worth flagging going the other direction: a JSON file is stricter than either language's native literal syntax for objects -- no comments, no trailing commas, keys must be double-quoted strings -- so both Python and JavaScript's parsers will reject a JSON string that happens to use, say, Python-style single-quoted strings or JavaScript-style unquoted keys, even though both of those would be perfectly valid in that language's own native object/dict literal syntax.
